mcqs.question: Does using `var` in Java (relying on inference) make the resulting code less type-safe than writing the type explicitly?
options: No — the compiler infers the type from the initializer and then checks everything downstream exactly as it would against an explicit annotation; inference only changes who writes the annotation
Yes — `var` disables static checking for that variable for the rest of the function
Yes — inferred variables are checked only at runtime, like a dynamically typed value
It depends on whether the variable is later reassigned to a different type
mcqs.explanation: Inference is purely a notational convenience — the compiler determines the type once from the initializer and enforces it identically to an explicit annotation for every subsequent use, with zero change in safety. It does not disable checking, does not push checking to runtime, and reassignment to an incompatible type is still a compile error either way.

mcqs.question: In Hindley-Milner inference for `let double = fun x -> x + x`, how does the algorithm determine `x`'s type without any annotation?
options: It defaults every unannotated parameter to a generic type variable and never narrows it further
It requires the caller to specify x's type at every call site instead of inferring it
It introduces a placeholder type for x, observes that x is used with +, and propagates the constraint that + imposes back onto that placeholder to resolve it to a numeric type
It looks at the variable name `x` and assumes it is always numeric by convention
mcqs.explanation: Hindley-Milner treats unannotated types as placeholders and solves for them via unification over the constraints the body's operations impose — here, `+` requiring a numeric type resolves x's placeholder. It doesn't default everything to an unconstrained generic (constraints do narrow types when present), doesn't require per-call-site annotation, and never uses variable names as a signal.

mcqs.question: Why do languages with powerful type inference (Kotlin, Rust) still require or strongly encourage explicit type annotations on public function signatures?
options: Because inference is technically incapable of handling function signatures at all
Because public function compilation is slower when inference is used
Because explicit annotations are mandatory syntax with no exceptions in any statically typed language
Because a public signature is a contract with every caller, and inferring it from the current implementation would let the contract silently drift whenever the implementation changes
mcqs.explanation: A public signature needs to stay stable for callers, so annotating it explicitly makes any contract change visible in the diff, whereas an inferred signature could shift silently with an implementation change. Inference is fully capable of handling function signatures internally (as Hindley-Milner shows), it's not a compilation-speed issue, and it isn't a universal mandatory-syntax rule across all statically typed languages.

mcqs.question: A public function's return type is inferred rather than explicitly annotated. A later refactor adds a branch that can return null, silently widening the inferred type. What is the actual risk this creates?
options: The function's contract for every caller changes without that change being visible as an explicit signature edit in the diff
The program will fail to compile until the annotation is added manually
Nothing — inferred types can never widen once a function is first compiled
The function becomes dynamically typed as soon as its inferred type changes
mcqs.explanation: The real risk named in this pitfall is a silent contract change: callers relying on the old, narrower inferred type get no signal from the diff that the return type has widened. The program still compiles fine (the widened type is consistent with the new branch), inferred types absolutely can widen across refactors, and the function remains statically typed throughout — it never becomes dynamic.

mcqs.question: Why can Hindley-Milner's type error messages sometimes point at a location far from the actual mistake, while local inference's errors are usually easy to diagnose on the spot?
options: Hindley-Milner deliberately obfuscates error locations to protect proprietary algorithms
Local inference only ever fails due to syntax errors, never type errors

The constraint solver only discovers a contradiction once enough constraints have accumulated across the function, so the reported location is where propagation failed, not necessarily where the mistake originated; local inference only ever looks at one line
Hindley-Milner does not produce any error messages at all when inference fails
mcqs.explanation: Whole-program constraint solving can surface a contradiction only after constraints from multiple parts of the code have combined, so the reported failure site can be distant from the true source; local inference's narrow one-line scope avoids this entirely. There is no deliberate obfuscation, local inference can and does fail on genuine type mismatches (not just syntax), and Hindley-Milner does produce error messages, just sometimes confusing ones.
